The takuapu is an idiophone used by the Guaraní of South America, made from a hollow bamboo tube and classed as Hornbostel–Sachs 1.11.231 (individual struck tube). The instrument can be up to two metres long and twenty to thirty centimetres in diameter, keeps the bamboo node nearest the ground, is often drilled at the side, and sometimes has pebbles put inside. The player holds it at the middle and drops it vertically so that it strikes the ground, producing a low sound; outdoors or on muddy ground a wooden board is often laid down to make it louder. It was originally played only by women in Guaraní religious rites, with dance and song, while the men accompanied on maracas.
塔誇普鼓的基本操作順序為：演奏者以手握住竹管中段，使管身保持垂直，再將管身落下，: The basic procedure for the takuapu is this: the player grips the middle of the bamboo tube, keeps it vertical, then lets it fall so that it strikes the ground, the impact producing a low sound. When playing outdoors or on mud, a wooden board can be placed on the ground to make the sound louder. All the internal nodes except the one near the ground are removed, so the tube is closed at the bottom; holes are often drilled in the side to change the sound, and sometimes a handful of small stones is put inside for a rattling sound. For a beginner the only points are the grip, the vertical drop and the strike on the ground; the sources describe no other teaching material or method.
塔誇普鼓見於瓜拉尼人的儀式場合，傳統上由女性演奏，配合舞蹈與歌唱；儀式歌唱中，女: The takuapu appears in Guaraní ritual settings and is traditionally played by women, with dance and song; in ritual song the women beat the takuapu while the men shake rattles. Formosa province in Argentina is traditional Guaraní country, and local ensembles also use the drum in performance, and there is footage of the takuapu accompanying Guaraní traditional song. Other places have similar bamboo drums, for example in Trinidad and Tobago, where men play them in processions.
塔誇普鼓起源於南美洲亞馬遜盆地，是瓜拉尼人在與自然環保相處的長期實踐中發展出的打: The takuapu comes from the Amazon basin of South America and is a percussion instrument the Guaraní developed over long practice of living with nature and caring for their environment. Making use of the abundant local bamboo, the Guaraní chose species such as takuára and takuarusu to make hollow tubes, and a distinctive playing tradition grew up. The name combines the Guaraní words takua (bamboo) and pu (sound), reflecting the indigenous use of natural materials.
塔誇普鼓音色沉厚而原始，具有明顯的暗沉質感，帶有空洞竹製樂器特有的溫潤感。其音域: The takuapu sounds deep and primitive, with a marked darkness and the warmth peculiar to a hollow bamboo instrument. Its range is low to middle, and the sound it makes striking the ground is profound and carrying. Its resonance is unusual: the air shaking inside the hollow tube and the vibration of the bamboo wall work on each other, giving a low resonance like an African drum or a native war drum, but more ethereal. Beside Western percussion it is closer to the depth of a bass drum, yet with the clean, clear texture of a bamboo instrument. Its sound has both a primitive roughness and the mildness of natural material, and it suits a sacred, solemn ritual atmosphere.

Its deep tone is seen as a medium that connects with the earth. Today the instrument is spreading to other parts of South America and into the international folk music scene, drawing attention from musicians and lovers of culture around the world, and it has become an important emblem of Guaraní cultural heritage.
